Part 2 · Linear Algebra and Geometry · Channels A, B and C · Lesson L04

Polynomials

Polynomials like x3−2x+5x^3 - 2x + 5x3−2x+5 can be added, multiplied and divided with remainder, just like integers. Their roots correspond to the factors x−ax - ax−a and are counted with multiplicity: a polynomial of degree nnn has at most nnn of them, and in the complex numbers exactly nnn (fundamental theorem of algebra). They are needed throughout the course: eigenvalues, determinants with a parameter and spaces of polynomials Rk[x]\R_k[x]Rk​[x] all start from here.

The lesson in 8 points

  • A polynomial in one variable, written in normal form, is p(x)=anxn+⋯+a1x+a0p(x) = a_nx^n + \dots + a_1x + a_0p(x)=an​xn+⋯+a1​x+a0​ with an≠0a_n \neq 0an​=0; the number nnn is its degree. R[x]\R[x]R[x] and C[x]\C[x]C[x] are the polynomials with real and complex coefficients, Rk[x]\R_k[x]Rk​[x] the real ones of degree at most kkk.
  • As among the integers, you can divide with remainder: given p(x)p(x)p(x) and d(x)≠0d(x) \neq 0d(x)=0 there exist unique q(x)q(x)q(x) and r(x)r(x)r(x) with p(x)=q(x)d(x)+r(x)p(x) = q(x)d(x) + r(x)p(x)=q(x)d(x)+r(x) and the degree of rrr smaller than the degree of ddd. If r=0r = 0r=0 we say that d(x)d(x)d(x) divides p(x)p(x)p(x).
  • A number aaa is a root of p(x)p(x)p(x) if p(a)=0p(a) = 0p(a)=0. Proposition 4.2: aaa is a root if and only if (x−a)(x - a)(x−a) divides p(x)p(x)p(x). Moreover the remainder of the division by x−ax - ax−a is exactly p(a)p(a)p(a).
  • The multiplicity of a root aaa is the largest kkk for which (x−a)k(x - a)^k(x−a)k divides p(x)p(x)p(x): in (x−1)3(x+1)(x - 1)^3(x + 1)(x−1)3(x+1) the root 111 has multiplicity 333.
  • Theorem 4.6: a polynomial of degree n≥1n \ge 1n≥1 has at most nnn roots, counted with multiplicity. Among the reals there may be fewer: x2+1x^2 + 1x2+1 has none.
  • Fundamental theorem of algebra (4.8): a polynomial with complex coefficients of degree nnn has exactly nnn roots in the complex numbers, counted with multiplicity.

§1

Monomials and polynomials

p. 15

The handouts describe polynomials as particularly simple functions, obtained by combining numbers and variables with only the operations +++, −-− and ⋅\cdot⋅. No divisions by a variable, no roots of variables, no negative exponents: x2+3x^2 + 3x2+3 is a polynomial, 1x\frac 1xx1​ and x\sqrt xx​ are not.

Monomials

A monomial is an expression with a numerical part, the coefficient, and a literal part, made of variables raised to natural exponents. The degree of a monomial is the sum of the exponents of the variables.

MonomialCoefficientLiteral partDegree
4x4x4x444xxx111
−2xy-2xy−2xy−2-2−2xyxyxy1+1=21 + 1 = 21+1=2
5 x3\sqrt 5\,x^35​x35\sqrt 55​x3x^3x3333
777777none000

These are the three examples of the handouts, plus the last row: a monomial of degree zero is simply a number.

Polynomials and normal form

A polynomial is a sum of monomials, for example 7+3x2−2 y37 + 3x^2 - \sqrt 2\,y^37+3x2−2​y3 (here there are two variables, xxx and yyy). The same polynomial can be written in many ways; to compare them a standard way of writing is used.

Definition · Normal form and degree (p. 15)

A polynomial is reduced to normal form if it is written as a sum of monomials with different literal parts and non-zero coefficients, or it is the polynomial 000. To reduce it to normal form it is enough to collect the monomials with the same literal part and then eliminate those with zero coefficient.

The degree of a polynomial written in normal form is the largest degree of its monomials.

Example · Reduce, then read the degree

3x2+2x−x2+5−2x3x^2 + 2x - x^2 + 5 - 2x3x2+2x−x2+5−2x: collect the similar monomials, (3−1)x2+(2−2)x+5=2x2+0x+5(3 - 1)x^2 + (2 - 2)x + 5 = 2x^2 + 0x + 5(3−1)x2+(2−2)x+5=2x2+0x+5, and eliminate the one with zero coefficient. Normal form: 2x2+52x^2 + 52x2+5, degree 222.

7+3x2−2 y37 + 3x^2 - \sqrt 2\,y^37+3x2−2​y3 is already in normal form: the monomials have degrees 000, 222 and 333, so the polynomial has degree 333.

Pitfall · The degree is read after reducing

(x+1)2−x2(x + 1)^2 - x^2(x+1)2−x2 looks like a second-degree polynomial, but expanding you get x2+2x+1−x2=2x+1x^2 + 2x + 1 - x^2 = 2x + 1x2+2x+1−x2=2x+1: the degree is 111. First reduce to normal form, then look at the degree.

Polynomials in one variable

In the course we are interested above all in polynomials with a single variable xxx, denoted by p(x)p(x)p(x) or simply by ppp. Ordering the monomials from the highest degree to the lowest you get the expression

p(x)=anxn+⋯+a1x+a0,an≠0,p(x) = a_nx^n + \dots + a_1x + a_0, \qquad a_n \neq 0,p(x)=an​xn+⋯+a1​x+a0​,an​=0,

where nnn is the degree of p(x)p(x)p(x). The numbers an,…,a1,a0a_n, \dots, a_1, a_0an​,…,a1​,a0​ are the coefficients; a0a_0a0​ is called the constant term. Two examples from the handouts:

  • x3−2x+5x^3 - 2x + 5x3−2x+5 has degree 333, with a3=1a_3 = 1a3​=1, a2=0a_2 = 0a2​=0 (the term in x2x^2x2 is missing), a1=−2a_1 = -2a1​=−2, a0=5a_0 = 5a0​=5;
  • 4x2−74x^2 - 74x2−7 has degree 222, with a2=4a_2 = 4a2​=4, a1=0a_1 = 0a1​=0, a0=−7a_0 = -7a0​=−7.

A polynomial of degree zero is simply a number a0≠0a_0 \neq 0a0​=0.

Definition · The sets of polynomials (p. 15)

R[x]\R[x]R[x] is the set of polynomials with coefficients in R\RR in which a single variable xxx appears, and C[x]\C[x]C[x] the set of polynomials with coefficients in C\CC in which a single variable xxx appears. Rk[x]\R_k[x]Rk​[x] denotes the polynomials in R[x]\R[x]R[x] that have degree ≤k\le k≤k (similarly Ck[x]\C_k[x]Ck​[x]).

Piece by piece:

  • R[x]⊂C[x]\R[x] \subset \C[x]R[x]⊂C[x], because real numbers are complex. For example x2+1x^2 + 1x2+1 belongs to both, while ix+1ix + 1ix+1 belongs to C[x]\C[x]C[x] but not to R[x]\R[x]R[x].
  • Rk[x]\R_k[x]Rk​[x] contains all the real polynomials of degree at most kkk, including those of lower degree and the zero polynomial. For example R2[x]={ax2+bx+c∣a,b,c∈R}\R_2[x] = \{ax^2 + bx + c \mid a, b, c \in \R\}R2​[x]={ax2+bx+c∣a,b,c∈R} contains x2−3x^2 - 3x2−3, 5x5x5x, 777 and 000 (with a=0a = 0a=0 the degree drops), but not x3x^3x3.
  • From lesson L05 on, Rk[x]\R_k[x]Rk​[x] will be one of the main examples of a vector space: in the exam papers there are often questions on sets like {p(x)∈R3[x]∣p(6)=0}\{p(x) \in \R_3[x] \mid p(6) = 0\}{p(x)∈R3​[x]∣p(6)=0}.

Beyond the handouts · the zero polynomial and the degree of products

The polynomial 000 has no monomials, so its degree is not defined (some books give it degree −∞-\infty−∞). For two non-zero polynomials two useful rules hold:

  • deg⁡(pq)=deg⁡p+deg⁡q\deg(pq) = \deg p + \deg qdeg(pq)=degp+degq: the terms of highest degree multiply, anxn⋅bmxm=anbm xn+ma_nx^n \cdot b_mx^m = a_nb_m\,x^{n + m}an​xn⋅bm​xm=an​bm​xn+m, and anbm≠0a_nb_m \neq 0an​bm​=0. For example (x2+1)(x3−x)(x^2 + 1)(x^3 - x)(x2+1)(x3−x) has degree 555.
  • deg⁡(p+q)≤\deg(p + q) \ledeg(p+q)≤ the larger of deg⁡p\deg pdegp and deg⁡q\deg qdegq, and it can be smaller if the highest terms cancel out, as in the pitfall above.

Martelli also calls a polynomial with an=1a_n = 1an​=1 monic.

§2

Division with remainder

pp. 15–16

Polynomials resemble integers: they can be added and multiplied, and divisions with remainder can be done. Among the integers, dividing 444444 by 666 you find quotient 777 and remainder 222:

44=7⋅6+2,44 = 7 \cdot 6 + 2,44=7⋅6+2,

and the remainder 222 is smaller than the divisor 666. For polynomials "smaller" means "of lower degree".

Proposition · Division with remainder (p. 16)

Given two polynomials p(x)p(x)p(x) (the dividend) and d(x)≠0d(x) \neq 0d(x)=0 (the divisor), there always exist, and they are unique, two polynomials q(x)q(x)q(x) (the quotient) and r(x)r(x)r(x) (the remainder) such that

p(x)=q(x)d(x)+r(x),p(x) = q(x)d(x) + r(x),p(x)=q(x)d(x)+r(x),

with the property that the remainder r(x)r(x)r(x) has degree strictly smaller than the divisor d(x)d(x)d(x).

Piece by piece:

  • d(x)≠0d(x) \neq 0d(x)=0: as among numbers, you do not divide by zero.
  • The condition on the degree is what makes quotient and remainder unique. Without it you could write infinitely many equalities of the form p=qd+rp = qd + rp=qd+r (you find an example in the quiz).
  • The remainder can be the polynomial 000: it is the important case, the one of divisibility.

The handouts say that divisions are done with pen and paper using the same procedure as for integers. Here it is, step by step.

Method · Long division

  1. Write dividend and divisor in order of decreasing degree; in the dividend put 000 in place of the missing degrees.
  2. Divide the highest-degree term of the dividend by the highest-degree term of the divisor: it is the first term of the quotient.
  3. Multiply the divisor by this term and subtract the result from the dividend: the highest term cancels out.
  4. Repeat steps 2 and 3 with the polynomial obtained, until its degree becomes smaller than the degree of the divisor. What is left is the remainder.
  5. Check: q(x)d(x)+r(x)q(x)d(x) + r(x)q(x)d(x)+r(x) must give back p(x)p(x)p(x).

Example · The handouts' example: x3+1x^3 + 1x3+1 divided by x2−1x^2 - 1x2−1

  1. x3:x2=xx^3 : x^2 = xx3:x2=x: the quotient starts with xxx.
  2. x⋅(x2−1)=x3−xx \cdot (x^2 - 1) = x^3 - xx⋅(x2−1)=x3−x, and (x3+1)−(x3−x)=x+1(x^3 + 1) - (x^3 - x) = x + 1(x3+1)−(x3−x)=x+1.
  3. x+1x + 1x+1 has degree 111, smaller than the degree 222 of the divisor: we stop.

Quotient q(x)=xq(x) = xq(x)=x, remainder r(x)=x+1r(x) = x + 1r(x)=x+1:

x3+1=x(x2−1)+(x+1).x^3 + 1 = x\left(x^2 - 1\right) + (x + 1).x3+1=x(x2−1)+(x+1).

Check: x3−x+x+1=x3+1x^3 - x + x + 1 = x^3 + 1x3−x+x+1=x3+1.

Example · A division in two steps: 2x3+3x2−x+52x^3 + 3x^2 - x + 52x3+3x2−x+5 divided by x2−x+1x^2 - x + 1x2−x+1

  1. 2x3:x2=2x2x^3 : x^2 = 2x2x3:x2=2x. Then 2x(x2−x+1)=2x3−2x2+2x2x(x^2 - x + 1) = 2x^3 - 2x^2 + 2x2x(x2−x+1)=2x3−2x2+2x, and subtracting:
    (2x3+3x2−x+5)−(2x3−2x2+2x)=5x2−3x+5.(2x^3 + 3x^2 - x + 5) - (2x^3 - 2x^2 + 2x) = 5x^2 - 3x + 5.(2x3+3x2−x+5)−(2x3−2x2+2x)=5x2−3x+5.
  2. The degree is still 222, so we continue: 5x2:x2=55x^2 : x^2 = 55x2:x2=5. Then 5(x2−x+1)=5x2−5x+55(x^2 - x + 1) = 5x^2 - 5x + 55(x2−x+1)=5x2−5x+5, and subtracting:
    (5x2−3x+5)−(5x2−5x+5)=2x.(5x^2 - 3x + 5) - (5x^2 - 5x + 5) = 2x.(5x2−3x+5)−(5x2−5x+5)=2x.
  3. 2x2x2x has degree 1<21 < 21<2: end.

Quotient q(x)=2x+5q(x) = 2x + 5q(x)=2x+5, remainder r(x)=2xr(x) = 2xr(x)=2x. Check: (2x+5)(x2−x+1)+2x=2x3−2x2+2x+5x2−5x+5+2x=2x3+3x2−x+5(2x + 5)(x^2 - x + 1) + 2x = 2x^3 - 2x^2 + 2x + 5x^2 - 5x + 5 + 2x = 2x^3 + 3x^2 - x + 5(2x+5)(x2−x+1)+2x=2x3−2x2+2x+5x2−5x+5+2x=2x3+3x2−x+5.

When a polynomial divides another

Among the integers, 777 divides 141414 but not 151515: the division of 141414 by 777 has zero remainder, that of 151515 by 777 does not. For polynomials the same word is used.

Definition · Divisibility (p. 16)

If the division between two polynomials p(x)p(x)p(x) and d(x)d(x)d(x) has zero remainder, then p(x)=q(x)d(x)p(x) = q(x)d(x)p(x)=q(x)d(x) for some quotient q(x)q(x)q(x), and we say that d(x)d(x)d(x) divides p(x)p(x)p(x). The vertical bar ∣\mid∣ is used as a synonym of "divides":

9∣18,(x+1)∣(x3+1).9 \mid 18, \qquad (x + 1) \mid \left(x^3 + 1\right).9∣18,(x+1)∣(x3+1).

Let us check the second example with the long division of x3+0x2+0x+1x^3 + 0x^2 + 0x + 1x3+0x2+0x+1 by x+1x + 1x+1:

  1. x3:x=x2x^3 : x = x^2x3:x=x2; x2(x+1)=x3+x2x^2(x + 1) = x^3 + x^2x2(x+1)=x3+x2; subtracting, what is left is −x2+0x+1-x^2 + 0x + 1−x2+0x+1.
  2. −x2:x=−x-x^2 : x = -x−x2:x=−x; −x(x+1)=−x2−x-x(x + 1) = -x^2 - x−x(x+1)=−x2−x; subtracting, what is left is x+1x + 1x+1.
  3. x:x=1x : x = 1x:x=1; 1⋅(x+1)=x+11 \cdot (x + 1) = x + 11⋅(x+1)=x+1; subtracting, what is left is 000.

The remainder is zero, and the quotient is x2−x+1x^2 - x + 1x2−x+1: indeed, as the handouts note, (x3+1)=(x2−x+1)(x+1)\left(x^3 + 1\right) = \left(x^2 - x + 1\right)(x + 1)(x3+1)=(x2−x+1)(x+1).

Pitfall · The zeros and the stopping condition

If some degrees are missing in the dividend, as in x3+1x^3 + 1x3+1, you must write the zeros (x3+0x2+0x+1x^3 + 0x^2 + 0x + 1x3+0x2+0x+1), otherwise you subtract terms of different degrees. And you stop when the degree of what is left is smaller than that of the divisor, not when "a number is left": dividing by x2−x+1x^2 - x + 1x2−x+1, the remainder 2x2x2x is perfectly fine.

§3

Ruffini's rule

beyond the handouts

When the divisor has the form x−ax - ax−a (degree 111), the long division can be written in a table that contains only the coefficients: it is Ruffini's rule (synthetic division). It is the fastest way to use Proposition 4.2 of the next section.

Method · Dividing p(x)p(x)p(x) by x−ax - ax−a with Ruffini

  1. Write the coefficients of p(x)p(x)p(x) in a row, from the highest degree to the constant term, with zeros for the missing degrees. Write aaa on the left. Watch out for the sign: to divide by x+2x + 2x+2 you use a=−2a = -2a=−2.
  2. Bring the first coefficient down to the last row.
  3. Multiply by aaa the last number written at the bottom, write the product in the next column (middle row) and add: the result goes at the bottom.
  4. Repeat until the last column. The last number at the bottom is the remainder; the others are the coefficients of the quotient, which has degree one less.

Example · 2x3−3x2+4x−52x^3 - 3x^2 + 4x - 52x3−3x2+4x−5 divided by x−2x - 2x−2

Coefficients 2,−3,4,−52, -3, 4, -52,−3,4,−5 and a=2a = 2a=2:

222−3-3−3444−5-5−5
a=2a = 2a=2444222121212
222111666777

Column by column: bring down the 222; 2⋅2=42 \cdot 2 = 42⋅2=4 and −3+4=1-3 + 4 = 1−3+4=1; 1⋅2=21 \cdot 2 = 21⋅2=2 and 4+2=64 + 2 = 64+2=6; 6⋅2=126 \cdot 2 = 126⋅2=12 and −5+12=7-5 + 12 = 7−5+12=7. So quotient q(x)=2x2+x+6q(x) = 2x^2 + x + 6q(x)=2x2+x+6 and remainder 777:

2x3−3x2+4x−5=(2x2+x+6)(x−2)+7.2x^3 - 3x^2 + 4x - 5 = (2x^2 + x + 6)(x - 2) + 7.2x3−3x2+4x−5=(2x2+x+6)(x−2)+7.

Note: p(2)=16−12+8−5=7p(2) = 16 - 12 + 8 - 5 = 7p(2)=16−12+8−5=7, exactly the remainder. It is not a coincidence: the next section explains it.

With the tool below you can repeat the division with other polynomials and other values of aaa (the coefficients are written from the highest degree, separated by spaces). The button Factor with the rational roots tries all the candidates ±divisors of the constant termdivisors of the leading coefficient\pm\frac{\text{divisors of the constant term}}{\text{divisors of the leading coefficient}}±divisors of the leading coefficientdivisors of the constant term​ and factors the polynomial: try it with 1 -6 11 -6 and with 1 -1 -3 5 -2.

§4

Roots of a polynomial

p. 16

If p(x)p(x)p(x) is a polynomial and aaa is a number, p(a)p(a)p(a) is the number you get by substituting aaa in place of xxx. For example, if p(x)=x2−3p(x) = x^2 - 3p(x)=x2−3, then p(−2)=(−2)2−3=4−3=1p(-2) = (-2)^2 - 3 = 4 - 3 = 1p(−2)=(−2)2−3=4−3=1, p(0)=−3p(0) = -3p(0)=−3 and p(3)=3−3=0p(\sqrt 3) = 3 - 3 = 0p(3​)=3−3=0.

Definition 4.1

A number aaa is a root of a polynomial p(x)p(x)p(x) if p(a)=0p(a) = 0p(a)=0.

In other words, the roots of p(x)p(x)p(x) are the solutions of the equation p(x)=0p(x) = 0p(x)=0. Some examples:

  • −1-1−1 is a root of p(x)=x3+1p(x) = x^3 + 1p(x)=x3+1, because p(−1)=(−1)3+1=0p(-1) = (-1)^3 + 1 = 0p(−1)=(−1)3+1=0 (example from the handouts); instead 222 is not, because p(2)=9p(2) = 9p(2)=9;
  • 3\sqrt 33​ and −3-\sqrt 3−3​ are roots of x2−3x^2 - 3x2−3;
  • iii is a root of x2+1x^2 + 1x2+1, because i2+1=−1+1=0i^2 + 1 = -1 + 1 = 0i2+1=−1+1=0: roots can be complex numbers, and to check them you need the computations of lessons L02 and L03.

The handouts recall that finding the roots of a polynomial is one of the most classical problems of algebra. The criterion that follows links the roots to division.

§5

Roots and factors: Proposition 4.2

pp. 16–17

Proposition 4.2

The number aaa is a root of p(x)p(x)p(x) if and only if (x−a)∣p(x)(x - a) \mid p(x)(x−a)∣p(x).

Proof (from the handouts, with every step explained).

  1. Divide p(x)p(x)p(x) by (x−a)(x - a)(x−a): by division with remainder, p(x)=q(x)(x−a)+r(x)p(x) = q(x)(x - a) + r(x)p(x)=q(x)(x−a)+r(x), with q(x)q(x)q(x) the quotient and r(x)r(x)r(x) the remainder.
  2. The degree of r(x)r(x)r(x) is strictly smaller than that of x−ax - ax−a, which is 111. So r(x)r(x)r(x) has degree zero (or it is the zero polynomial): it is a constant, which we write r0r_0r0​. Then
    p(x)=q(x)(x−a)+r0.p(x) = q(x)(x - a) + r_0.p(x)=q(x)(x−a)+r0​.
  3. Substitute aaa in place of xxx: the factor a−aa - aa−a vanishes, and what is left is
    p(a)=q(a)(a−a)+r0=0+r0=r0.p(a) = q(a)(a - a) + r_0 = 0 + r_0 = r_0.p(a)=q(a)(a−a)+r0​=0+r0​=r0​.
  4. So aaa is a root of p(x)p(x)p(x) (that is p(a)=0p(a) = 0p(a)=0) if and only if r0=0r_0 = 0r0​=0.
  5. On the other hand r0=0r_0 = 0r0​=0 if and only if the division by x−ax - ax−a has zero remainder, that is if and only if (x−a)(x - a)(x−a) divides p(x)p(x)p(x). □\square□

The idea · the remainder is the value

Step 3 says something more than the statement: the remainder of the division of p(x)p(x)p(x) by x−ax - ax−a is p(a)p(a)p(a). It is what you saw with Ruffini: dividing by x−2x - 2x−2 the remainder was 7=p(2)7 = p(2)7=p(2). So to know whether aaa is a root it is enough to compute p(a)p(a)p(a); and to know the remainder of the division by x−ax - ax−a you do not need to do the division.

Method · Factoring a polynomial starting from a root

  1. Look for a root aaa by trying simple numbers: 000, ±1\pm 1±1, ±2\pm 2±2, … If the coefficients are integers, an integer root divides the constant term (see the box below).
  2. Divide by x−ax - ax−a with Ruffini: p(x)=(x−a)q(x)p(x) = (x - a)q(x)p(x)=(x−a)q(x), with q(x)q(x)q(x) of degree one less.
  3. Repeat with q(x)q(x)q(x). When you reach degree two use the formula with Δ\DeltaΔ.

Example · x3−6x2+11x−6x^3 - 6x^2 + 11x - 6x3−6x2+11x−6

  1. I try x=1x = 1x=1: 1−6+11−6=01 - 6 + 11 - 6 = 01−6+11−6=0. So 111 is a root and (x−1)(x - 1)(x−1) divides the polynomial.
  2. Ruffini with a=1a = 1a=1 on the coefficients 1,−6,11,−61, -6, 11, -61,−6,11,−6: bring down 111; 1−6=−51 - 6 = -51−6=−5; −5+11=6-5 + 11 = 6−5+11=6; 6−6=06 - 6 = 06−6=0. Quotient x2−5x+6x^2 - 5x + 6x2−5x+6, remainder 000.
  3. x2−5x+6=(x−2)(x−3)x^2 - 5x + 6 = (x - 2)(x - 3)x2−5x+6=(x−2)(x−3): two numbers with sum 555 and product 666.

So x3−6x2+11x−6=(x−1)(x−2)(x−3)x^3 - 6x^2 + 11x - 6 = (x - 1)(x - 2)(x - 3)x3−6x2+11x−6=(x−1)(x−2)(x−3), with roots 111, 222, 333.

Beyond the handouts · rational roots

If p(x)p(x)p(x) has integer coefficients and uv\frac uvvu​ is a rational root in lowest terms, then uuu divides the constant term a0a_0a0​ and vvv divides the leading coefficient ana_nan​. In particular, if an=1a_n = 1an​=1, every rational root is an integer that divides a0a_0a0​. For x3−6x2+11x−6x^3 - 6x^2 + 11x - 6x3−6x2+11x−6 the candidates were only ±1,±2,±3,±6\pm 1, \pm 2, \pm 3, \pm 6±1,±2,±3,±6. The reason: from p(uv)=0p\left(\frac uv\right) = 0p(vu​)=0, multiplying by vnv^nvn, you get anun+an−1un−1v+⋯+a0vn=0a_nu^n + a_{n-1}u^{n-1}v + \dots + a_0v^n = 0an​un+an−1​un−1v+⋯+a0​vn=0; all the terms except the last are multiples of uuu, so a0vna_0v^na0​vn is one too, and since uuu and vvv have no common factors, uuu divides a0a_0a0​. In the same way vvv divides ana_nan​.

§6

Multiplicity

p. 17

A root can appear "several times". In (x−2)2=(x−2)(x−2)(x - 2)^2 = (x - 2)(x - 2)(x−2)2=(x−2)(x−2) the factor x−2x - 2x−2 is there twice.

Definition 4.3

The multiplicity of a root aaa of a polynomial p(x)p(x)p(x) is the largest number kkk such that (x−a)k(x - a)^k(x−a)k divides p(x)p(x)p(x).

Informally, the handouts say, the multiplicity of aaa measures "how many times" aaa is a root of p(x)p(x)p(x). A root of multiplicity 111 is called simple, of multiplicity 222 double, of multiplicity 333 triple.

Example 4.4 · Multiplicity 111 and 222

The polynomial x3−1x^3 - 1x3−1 has the root 111 with multiplicity 111, because

x3−1=(x−1)(x2+x+1)x^3 - 1 = (x - 1)\left(x^2 + x + 1\right)x3−1=(x−1)(x2+x+1)

and (x−1)(x - 1)(x−1) does not divide x2+x+1x^2 + x + 1x2+x+1, simply because 111 is not a root of x2+x+1x^2 + x + 1x2+x+1: indeed 1+1+1=3≠01 + 1 + 1 = 3 \neq 01+1+1=3=0.

Similarly the polynomial x3−2x2+x=x(x2−2x+1)=(x−1)2xx^3 - 2x^2 + x = x\left(x^2 - 2x + 1\right) = (x - 1)^2xx3−2x2+x=x(x2−2x+1)=(x−1)2x has the root 111 with multiplicity 222 and the root 000 with multiplicity 111.

Example 4.5 · In the product the multiplicities add up

The polynomials q1(x)=x2−2x+1q_1(x) = x^2 - 2x + 1q1​(x)=x2−2x+1 and q2(x)=x2−1q_2(x) = x^2 - 1q2​(x)=x2−1 can be written

q1(x)=(x−1)2,q2(x)=(x+1)(x−1).q_1(x) = (x - 1)^2, \qquad q_2(x) = (x + 1)(x - 1).q1​(x)=(x−1)2,q2​(x)=(x+1)(x−1).

The first has the root 111 with multiplicity 222; the second has the roots −1-1−1 and 111, both with multiplicity 111. The product

p(x)=q1(x)q2(x)=(x−1)3(x+1)p(x) = q_1(x)q_2(x) = (x - 1)^3(x + 1)p(x)=q1​(x)q2​(x)=(x−1)3(x+1)

has the root 111 with multiplicity 2+1=32 + 1 = 32+1=3 and the root −1-1−1 with multiplicity 111.

When the polynomial is not already factored, the multiplicity is found by dividing several times.

Method · Computing the multiplicity of a root aaa

Divide p(x)p(x)p(x) by x−ax - ax−a (with Ruffini). If the quotient still has aaa as a root, divide again. Continue until aaa is no longer a root of the quotient: the number of divisions done is the multiplicity.

Example · p(x)=x4−x3−3x2+5x−2p(x) = x^4 - x^3 - 3x^2 + 5x - 2p(x)=x4−x3−3x2+5x−2 and the root 111

p(1)=1−1−3+5−2=0p(1) = 1 - 1 - 3 + 5 - 2 = 0p(1)=1−1−3+5−2=0, so 111 is a root.

  1. Ruffini with a=1a = 1a=1 on 1,−1,−3,5,−21, -1, -3, 5, -21,−1,−3,5,−2: at the bottom 1,0,−3,21, 0, -3, 21,0,−3,2 and remainder 000. Quotient x3−3x+2x^3 - 3x + 2x3−3x+2.
  2. 1−3+2=01 - 3 + 2 = 01−3+2=0: 111 is still a root. Ruffini on 1,0,−3,21, 0, -3, 21,0,−3,2: at the bottom 1,1,−21, 1, -21,1,−2 and remainder 000. Quotient x2+x−2x^2 + x - 2x2+x−2.
  3. 1+1−2=01 + 1 - 2 = 01+1−2=0: still a root. Ruffini on 1,1,−21, 1, -21,1,−2: at the bottom 1,21, 21,2 and remainder 000. Quotient x+2x + 2x+2.
  4. 1+2=3≠01 + 2 = 3 \neq 01+2=3=0: 111 is not a root of x+2x + 2x+2. Stop.

Three divisions: the root 111 has multiplicity 333, and p(x)=(x−1)3(x+2)p(x) = (x - 1)^3(x + 2)p(x)=(x−1)3(x+2).

What you see in the graph (beyond the handouts)

For a real polynomial, the real roots are the points where the graph of y=p(x)y = p(x)y=p(x) touches the xxx axis. The multiplicity can be seen from the shape: at a root of odd multiplicity the graph crosses the axis, at a root of even multiplicity it touches it and turns back, because the factor (x−a)2(x - a)^2(x−a)2 does not change sign.

§7

How many roots: Theorem 4.6

p. 18

Theorem 4.6

A polynomial p(x)p(x)p(x) of degree n≥1n \ge 1n≥1 has at most nnn roots, counted with multiplicity.

"Counted with multiplicity" means that you add up, for each root, its multiplicity: (x−1)3(x+1)(x - 1)^3(x + 1)(x−1)3(x+1) has two different roots, but counted with multiplicity they are 3+1=43 + 1 = 43+1=4, as many as the degree. The theorem says that this sum never exceeds the degree.

The proof uses induction on the degree nnn, which you will see in detail in Discrete Mathematics: you prove the statement for n=1n = 1n=1 (base case), then you show that, if it holds for degree n−1n - 1n−1, it also holds for degree nnn (inductive step). So it holds for n=1n = 1n=1, hence for n=2n = 2n=2, hence for n=3n = 3n=3, and so on.

Proof · of Theorem 4.6

Base case, n=1n = 1n=1. The polynomial is p(x)=a1x+a0p(x) = a_1x + a_0p(x)=a1​x+a0​ with a1≠0a_1 \neq 0a1​=0, and p(x)=0p(x) = 0p(x)=0 means x=−a0a1x = -\frac{a_0}{a_1}x=−a1​a0​​: there is a single root, of multiplicity 111. The statement holds.

Inductive step. Suppose the statement is true for polynomials of degree n−1n - 1n−1 and take p(x)p(x)p(x) of degree nnn.

  1. If p(x)p(x)p(x) has no roots, there is nothing to prove: 0≤n0 \le n0≤n.
  2. If it has at least one root aaa, by Proposition 4.2 we can write p(x)=(x−a)q(x)p(x) = (x - a)q(x)p(x)=(x−a)q(x), and q(x)q(x)q(x) has degree n−1n - 1n−1 (the degrees of the factors add up).
  3. By the inductive hypothesis q(x)q(x)q(x) has at most n−1n - 1n−1 roots counted with multiplicity.
  4. The roots of p(x)p(x)p(x), counted with multiplicity, are exactly those of q(x)q(x)q(x) plus aaa. Indeed for b≠ab \neq ab=a we have p(b)=(b−a)q(b)p(b) = (b - a)q(b)p(b)=(b−a)q(b) with b−a≠0b - a \neq 0b−a=0, so p(b)=0p(b) = 0p(b)=0 if and only if q(b)=0q(b) = 0q(b)=0; and the multiplicity of aaa in ppp is the one in qqq plus one, as in Example 4.5.
  5. So p(x)p(x)p(x) has at most (n−1)+1=n(n - 1) + 1 = n(n−1)+1=n roots, counted with multiplicity. □\square□

Example 4.7 · Polynomials of the first and second degree

A polynomial of degree 111 is always of the form p(x)=ax+bp(x) = ax + bp(x)=ax+b with a≠0a \neq 0a=0, and always has a single root x=−bax = -\frac bax=−ab​.

A polynomial of degree 222 is of the form p(x)=ax2+bx+cp(x) = ax^2 + bx + cp(x)=ax2+bx+c with a≠0a \neq 0a=0, and its roots depend on the discriminant Δ=b2−4ac\Delta = b^2 - 4acΔ=b2−4ac in the following way.

  • If Δ>0\Delta > 0Δ>0, the polynomial p(x)p(x)p(x) has two distinct roots x±=−b±Δ2ax_\pm = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt\Delta}{2a}x±​=2a−b±Δ​​, both of multiplicity one.
  • If Δ=0\Delta = 0Δ=0, the polynomial p(x)p(x)p(x) has a single root x=−b2ax = -\frac b{2a}x=−2ab​, with multiplicity two.
  • If Δ<0\Delta < 0Δ<0, the polynomial p(x)p(x)p(x) has no real roots.

In particular, there are polynomials that have no real roots.

Three examples, one per case:

PolynomialΔ=b2−4ac\Delta = b^2 - 4acΔ=b2−4acReal rootsFactorisation
x2−5x+6x^2 - 5x + 6x2−5x+625−24=1>025 - 24 = 1 > 025−24=1>05±12\frac{5 \pm 1}225±1​, that is 333 and 222(x−2)(x−3)(x - 2)(x - 3)(x−2)(x−3)
x2−4x+4x^2 - 4x + 4x2−4x+416−16=016 - 16 = 016−16=042=2\frac 42 = 224​=2, double(x−2)2(x - 2)^2(x−2)2
x2+x+1x^2 + x + 1x2+x+11−4=−3<01 - 4 = -3 < 01−4=−3<0nonedoes not factor in R\RR

Beyond the handouts · where the formula comes from

You "complete the square". For a≠0a \neq 0a=0:

ax2+bx+c=a(x+b2a)2−Δ4a.ax^2 + bx + c = a\left(x + \frac b{2a}\right)^2 - \frac{\Delta}{4a}.ax2+bx+c=a(x+2ab​)2−4aΔ​.

(To check it, expand the square: a(x2+bax+b24a2)−b2−4ac4a=ax2+bx+ca\left(x^2 + \frac bax + \frac{b^2}{4a^2}\right) - \frac{b^2 - 4ac}{4a} = ax^2 + bx + ca(x2+ab​x+4a2b2​)−4ab2−4ac​=ax2+bx+c.) So p(x)=0p(x) = 0p(x)=0 is equivalent to (x+b2a)2=Δ4a2\left(x + \frac b{2a}\right)^2 = \frac\Delta{4a^2}(x+2ab​)2=4a2Δ​. If Δ>0\Delta > 0Δ>0 you take the square root of both sides, with both signs; if Δ=0\Delta = 0Δ=0 what is left is x=−b2ax = -\frac b{2a}x=−2ab​; if Δ<0\Delta < 0Δ<0 a real square would have to be negative, which is impossible. It is the proof of Proposition 1.3.8 of Martelli's book.

§8

The fundamental theorem of algebra

p. 18

The handouts thus arrive "at the real reason why we introduced complex numbers in this course".

Theorem 4.8 · Fundamental theorem of algebra

A polynomial p(x)p(x)p(x) with complex coefficients of degree nnn has exactly nnn roots, counted with multiplicity.

Piece by piece:

  • Theorem 4.6 said "at most nnn". In the complex numbers the inequality becomes an equality: the roots are always all there.
  • It also holds for polynomials with real coefficients, which are particular polynomials with complex coefficients: x2+1x^2 + 1x2+1 has no real roots, but it has the two complex roots iii and −i-i−i.
  • The handouts do not prove it: the most accessible proofs use tools from calculus that are far from the course.

Beyond the handouts · another form of the same theorem

In Martelli's book the fundamental theorem (Theorem 1.4.7) says that every non-constant polynomial with complex coefficients has at least one root; from this you obtain the handouts' version (Corollary 1.4.8) with the same induction as Theorem 4.6: once a root z1z_1z1​ is found, you write p(x)=(x−z1)q(x)p(x) = (x - z_1)q(x)p(x)=(x−z1​)q(x) and repeat on q(x)q(x)q(x). The final result can also be written as a factorisation into factors of degree one (Corollary 1.4.10):

p(x)=an(x−z1)(x−z2)⋯(x−zn),p(x) = a_n(x - z_1)(x - z_2)\cdots(x - z_n),p(x)=an​(x−z1​)(x−z2​)⋯(x−zn​),

where z1,…,znz_1, \dots, z_nz1​,…,zn​ are the roots repeated according to their multiplicity. For example x4−1=(x−1)(x+1)(x−i)(x+i)x^4 - 1 = (x - 1)(x + 1)(x - i)(x + i)x4−1=(x−1)(x+1)(x−i)(x+i).

§9

Second-degree equations in C

p. 19

Example 4.9 · The usual formula, in the complex numbers

For a second-degree polynomial p(x)=ax2+bx+cp(x) = ax^2 + bx + cp(x)=ax2+bx+c the two complex roots are found using the usual formula

x±=−b±Δ2a.x_\pm = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt\Delta}{2a}.x±​=2a−b±Δ​​.

This time, ±Δ\pm\sqrt\Delta±Δ​ denotes the two complex square roots of Δ\DeltaΔ, which always exist, as seen in lesson L03.

Here aaa, bbb, ccc can be complex, and then Δ\DeltaΔ too can be a complex number: the distinction "Δ>0\Delta > 0Δ>0, Δ=0\Delta = 0Δ=0, Δ<0\Delta < 0Δ<0" only makes sense if Δ\DeltaΔ is real.

Method · A second-degree equation in C\CC

  1. Read off aaa, bbb, ccc and compute Δ=b2−4ac\Delta = b^2 - 4acΔ=b2−4ac.
  2. Find the two square roots ±w\pm w±w of Δ\DeltaΔ: if Δ\DeltaΔ is a negative real number, ±w=±i∣Δ∣\pm w = \pm i\sqrt{|\Delta|}±w=±i∣Δ∣​; if Δ\DeltaΔ is complex, use the polar form or the method w=u+viw = u + viw=u+vi (lessons L02 and L03).
  3. The roots are x±=−b±w2ax_\pm = \frac{-b \pm w}{2a}x±​=2a−b±w​.
  4. Check by substituting, or with sum and product: x++x−=−bax_+ + x_- = -\frac bax+​+x−​=−ab​ and x+x−=cax_+x_- = \frac cax+​x−​=ac​.

x2+1x^2 + 1x2+1. a=1a = 1a=1, b=0b = 0b=0, c=1c = 1c=1, so Δ=−4\Delta = -4Δ=−4, whose square roots are ±2i\pm 2i±2i. The roots are x±=±2i2=±ix_\pm = \frac{\pm 2i}2 = \pm ix±​=2±2i​=±i.

x2+(1−i)x−ix^2 + (1 - i)x - ix2+(1−i)x−i. Here a=1a = 1a=1, b=1−ib = 1 - ib=1−i, c=−ic = -ic=−i, and

Δ=(1−i)2−4⋅1⋅(−i)=(1−2i+i2)+4i=−2i+4i=2i.\Delta = (1 - i)^2 - 4 \cdot 1 \cdot (-i) = (1 - 2i + i^2) + 4i = -2i + 4i = 2i.Δ=(1−i)2−4⋅1⋅(−i)=(1−2i+i2)+4i=−2i+4i=2i.

Check: i2+(1−i)i−i=−1+i+1−i=0i^2 + (1 - i)i - i = -1 + i + 1 - i = 0i2+(1−i)i−i=−1+i+1−i=0 and (−1)2+(1−i)(−1)−i=1−1+i−i=0(-1)^2 + (1 - i)(-1) - i = 1 - 1 + i - i = 0(−1)2+(1−i)(−1)−i=1−1+i−i=0.

Two more examples with the same method:

§10

Polynomials with real coefficients

p. 19

A polynomial of degree nnn has exactly nnn complex roots counted with multiplicity. If its coefficients are real, something more can be said.

Proposition 4.11

Let p(x)p(x)p(x) be a polynomial with real coefficients. If zzz is a complex root of p(x)p(x)p(x), then zˉ\bar zzˉ is also a root of p(x)p(x)p(x).

Proof (from the handouts, with the rules used).

  1. The polynomial is p(x)=anxn+⋯+a1x+a0p(x) = a_nx^n + \dots + a_1x + a_0p(x)=an​xn+⋯+a1​x+a0​, and by hypothesis the coefficients an,…,a0a_n, \dots, a_0an​,…,a0​ are all real.
  2. If zzz is a root, then p(z)=anzn+⋯+a1z+a0=0p(z) = a_nz^n + \dots + a_1z + a_0 = 0p(z)=an​zn+⋯+a1​z+a0​=0.
  3. Apply conjugation to both sides. The conjugate of a sum is the sum of the conjugates and the conjugate of a product is the product of the conjugates (exercise 2.5, lesson L02); in particular zk‾=zˉk\overline{z^k} = \bar z^kzk=zˉk. So
    an‾ zˉn+⋯+a1‾ zˉ+a0‾=0ˉ=0.\overline{a_n}\,\bar z^n + \dots + \overline{a_1}\,\bar z + \overline{a_0} = \bar 0 = 0.an​​zˉn+⋯+a1​​zˉ+a0​​=0ˉ=0.
  4. Since the coefficients are real, the conjugate of aia_iai​ is always aia_iai​ (lesson L02: z∈R  ⟺  z=zˉz \in \R \iff z = \bar zz∈R⟺z=zˉ). So
    anzˉn+⋯+a1zˉ+a0=0,a_n\bar z^n + \dots + a_1\bar z + a_0 = 0,an​zˉn+⋯+a1​zˉ+a0​=0,
    that is p(zˉ)=0p(\bar z) = 0p(zˉ)=0: zˉ\bar zzˉ too is a root of p(x)p(x)p(x). □\square□

Example · x3−1x^3 - 1x3−1 and the cube roots of unity

x3−1=(x−1)(x2+x+1)x^3 - 1 = (x - 1)(x^2 + x + 1)x3−1=(x−1)(x2+x+1) (Example 4.4). The factor x2+x+1x^2 + x + 1x2+x+1 has Δ=−3\Delta = -3Δ=−3, square roots ±i3\pm i\sqrt 3±i3​, so roots −1±i32\frac{-1 \pm i\sqrt 3}22−1±i3​​. The three roots of x3−1x^3 - 1x3−1 are 111 and the conjugate pair −12±32i-\frac 12 \pm \frac{\sqrt 3}2 i−21​±23​​i: they are the three cube roots of unity of lesson L03, and the triangle they form is symmetric with respect to the real axis.

Pitfall · The coefficients need to be real

In Example 4.10 the polynomial x2+(1−i)x−ix^2 + (1 - i)x - ix2+(1−i)x−i has the root iii, but −i-i−i is not a root: the roots are iii and −1-1−1. Proposition 4.11 does not apply, because the coefficient 1−i1 - i1−i is not real. In the same way, in problem 11 of the exam of 03/06/2026 a characteristic polynomial with complex coefficients had the root iii double and the root −i-i−i simple.

Beyond the handouts · three consequences

  • The non-real roots of a polynomial with real coefficients come in pairs z,zˉz, \bar zz,zˉ (with the same multiplicity, even though Proposition 4.11 alone does not say so). So there is an even number of them.
  • A polynomial with real coefficients of odd degree always has at least one real root: the nnn complex roots are an odd number, and the non-real ones an even number (Proposition 1.4.13 of Martelli's book).
  • For z=u+viz = u + viz=u+vi with v≠0v \neq 0v=0: (x−z)(x−zˉ)=x2−2ux+(u2+v2)(x - z)(x - \bar z) = x^2 - 2ux + (u^2 + v^2)(x−z)(x−zˉ)=x2−2ux+(u2+v2), a real polynomial of degree two with Δ=−4v2<0\Delta = -4v^2 < 0Δ=−4v2<0. This is why every real polynomial factors into real factors of degree one and of degree two with Δ<0\Delta < 0Δ<0 (Corollary 1.4.12). For example x3−1=(x−1)(x2+x+1)x^3 - 1 = (x - 1)(x^2 + x + 1)x3−1=(x−1)(x2+x+1) and x4−1=(x−1)(x+1)(x2+1)x^4 - 1 = (x - 1)(x + 1)(x^2 + 1)x4−1=(x−1)(x+1)(x2+1).

Beyond the handouts · where to find it in the book

In Martelli's book this lesson corresponds to §1.3 "Polinomi" (pp. 21–25: definition, division with remainder, roots, Proposition 1.3.2 = 4.2, multiplicity, Theorem 1.3.7 = 4.6, the second-degree formula with proof) and to parts 1.4.7 "Teorema fondamentale dell'algebra" and 1.4.8 "Polinomi a coefficienti reali" of §1.4 (pp. 31–33). The examples are the same as in the handouts (in Martelli the first division between integers is 26=2⋅11+426 = 2 \cdot 11 + 426=2⋅11+4). Exercise 1.12 (p. 37) links multiplicity to the derivative, which you will see in Calculus.

Here are the three questions of the first type, with the solution.

Example · Exam of 10/07/2025, question 1

Which of the following is a root of p(z)=z4+7z2+12p(z) = z^4 + 7z^2 + 12p(z)=z4+7z2+12? (a) z=−2iz = -2iz=−2i; (b) z=−2z = -2z=−2; (c) the polynomial has no roots; (d) z=3+4iz = 3 + 4iz=3+4i; (e) z=4z = 4z=4.

Solution. Only even powers appear: I set w=z2w = z^2w=z2 and get w2+7w+12=(w+3)(w+4)w^2 + 7w + 12 = (w + 3)(w + 4)w2+7w+12=(w+3)(w+4), with roots w=−3w = -3w=−3 and w=−4w = -4w=−4. So z2=−3z^2 = -3z2=−3 or z2=−4z^2 = -4z2=−4, that is z=±i3z = \pm i\sqrt 3z=±i3​ or z=±2iz = \pm 2iz=±2i. Answer (a). Answer (c) is false by the fundamental theorem (there are four roots); (b) and (e) are real, and for real zzz z4+7z2+12≥12>0z^4 + 7z^2 + 12 \ge 12 > 0z4+7z2+12≥12>0.

Example · Exam of 03/07/2026, question 7

Which of the following is a root of the polynomial p(z)=z3+2z2+z+2p(z) = z^3 + 2z^2 + z + 2p(z)=z3+2z2+z+2? (a) z=0z = 0z=0; (b) z=iz = iz=i; (c) z=1+iz = 1 + iz=1+i; (d) z=1z = 1z=1; (e) z3+2z2+z+2=0z^3 + 2z^2 + z + 2 = 0z3+2z2+z+2=0.

Solution. Factoring by grouping: p(z)=z2(z+2)+(z+2)=(z2+1)(z+2)p(z) = z^2(z + 2) + (z + 2) = (z^2 + 1)(z + 2)p(z)=z2(z+2)+(z+2)=(z2+1)(z+2). The roots are −2-2−2, iii, −i-i−i: answer (b). Without factoring, it is enough to substitute: p(i)=i3+2i2+i+2=−i−2+i+2=0p(i) = i^3 + 2i^2 + i + 2 = -i - 2 + i + 2 = 0p(i)=i3+2i2+i+2=−i−2+i+2=0, while p(0)=2p(0) = 2p(0)=2 and p(1)=6p(1) = 6p(1)=6. Answer (e) is not a number but the equation itself.

Example · Exam of 07/09/2026, question 1

Which of the following is a root of the polynomial p(z)=z4+5z2+4p(z) = z^4 + 5z^2 + 4p(z)=z4+5z2+4? (a) z=−3+iz = -3 + iz=−3+i; (b) z=1−iz = 1 - iz=1−i; (c) z=−1z = -1z=−1; (d) z=−2iz = -2iz=−2i; (e) the polynomial has no roots.

Solution. With t=z2t = z^2t=z2: t2+5t+4=(t+1)(t+4)t^2 + 5t + 4 = (t + 1)(t + 4)t2+5t+4=(t+1)(t+4), roots t=−1t = -1t=−1 and t=−4t = -4t=−4. So z2=−1z^2 = -1z2=−1 or z2=−4z^2 = -4z2=−4: z=±iz = \pm iz=±i and z=±2iz = \pm 2iz=±2i. Answer (d). Direct check: (−2i)2=−4(-2i)^2 = -4(−2i)2=−4 and (−2i)4=16(-2i)^4 = 16(−2i)4=16, so p(−2i)=16−20+4=0p(-2i) = 16 - 20 + 4 = 0p(−2i)=16−20+4=0.

Method · Finding the roots of a polynomial of degree 3 or 4 without a calculator

  1. In the quiz, substitute the answers: with p(i)p(i)p(i), p(2i)p(2i)p(2i), p(−1)p(-1)p(−1)… you find the right answer in a few computations.
  2. Only even powers (z4z^4z4, z2z^2z2, constant term): set t=z2t = z^2t=z2, solve the second-degree equation, then z=±tz = \pm\sqrt tz=±t​ (with ttt negative, ±i∣t∣\pm i\sqrt{|t|}±i∣t∣​).
  3. Factoring by grouping: z3+2z2+z+2=z2(z+2)+1⋅(z+2)z^3 + 2z^2 + z + 2 = z^2(z + 2) + 1 \cdot (z + 2)z3+2z2+z+2=z2(z+2)+1⋅(z+2).
  4. Try the integer roots among the divisors of the constant term, then divide with Ruffini.
  5. A second-degree factor is left: formula with Δ\DeltaΔ; if the coefficients are real and Δ<0\Delta < 0Δ<0, the two roots are conjugate.

Mistakes to avoid. Forgetting the zeros in Ruffini's table; getting the sign of aaa wrong (for x+2x + 2x+2 you use a=−2a = -2a=−2); stopping the division too early or too late; confusing the number of distinct roots with the number of roots counted with multiplicity; applying Proposition 4.11 to polynomials with complex coefficients; in biquadratic equations, forgetting the two opposite roots of each ttt.

Matters in the exam · The 4-page sheet

From this lesson: the scheme of long division and of Ruffini; "aaa is a root   ⟺  (x−a)∣p(x)\iff (x - a) \mid p(x)⟺(x−a)∣p(x), and the remainder of the division by x−ax - ax−a is p(a)p(a)p(a)"; multiplicity and the method of repeated divisions; Δ\DeltaΔ and the second-degree formula with complex ±Δ\pm\sqrt\Delta±Δ​; "real coefficients ⇒\Rightarrow⇒ non-real roots in conjugate pairs"; the substitution t=z2t = z^2t=z2 and factoring by grouping.

Quiz

like the exam
  1. Which of the following is a root of p(z)=z4+10z2+9p(z) = z^4 + 10z^2 + 9p(z)=z4+10z2+9?
    With t=z2t = z^2t=z2: t2+10t+9=(t+1)(t+9)t^2 + 10t + 9 = (t + 1)(t + 9)t2+10t+9=(t+1)(t+9), so z2=−1z^2 = -1z2=−1 or z2=−9z^2 = -9z2=−9, that is z=±iz = \pm iz=±i or z=±3iz = \pm 3iz=±3i. Check: (3i)2=−9(3i)^2 = -9(3i)2=−9, (3i)4=81(3i)^4 = 81(3i)4=81, and 81−90+9=081 - 90 + 9 = 081−90+9=0. For real zzz p(z)≥9p(z) \ge 9p(z)≥9; p(1+i)=5+20ip(1 + i) = 5 + 20ip(1+i)=5+20i. By the fundamental theorem the roots always exist. Similar to the exams of 07/09/2026 and 10/07/2025, question 1.
  2. Which of the following is a root of p(z)=z3−2z2+4z−8p(z) = z^3 - 2z^2 + 4z - 8p(z)=z3−2z2+4z−8?
    Factoring by grouping: p(z)=z2(z−2)+4(z−2)=(z2+4)(z−2)p(z) = z^2(z - 2) + 4(z - 2) = (z^2 + 4)(z - 2)p(z)=z2(z−2)+4(z−2)=(z2+4)(z−2), roots 222 and ±2i\pm 2i±2i. Check: (−2i)3=8i(-2i)^3 = 8i(−2i)3=8i and (−2i)2=−4(-2i)^2 = -4(−2i)2=−4, so p(−2i)=8i+8−8i−8=0p(-2i) = 8i + 8 - 8i - 8 = 0p(−2i)=8i+8−8i−8=0. Instead p(−2)=−32p(-2) = -32p(−2)=−32, p(4)=40p(4) = 40p(4)=40, p(2+2i)=−16+8ip(2 + 2i) = -16 + 8ip(2+2i)=−16+8i, p(1−i)=−6−2ip(1 - i) = -6 - 2ip(1−i)=−6−2i. Similar to the exam of 03/07/2026, question 7.
  3. What is the remainder of the division of x4−3x2+2x−1x^4 - 3x^2 + 2x - 1x4−3x2+2x−1 by x+1x + 1x+1? Write a number.
    -5
    The remainder of the division by x−ax - ax−a is p(a)p(a)p(a); here x+1=x−(−1)x + 1 = x - (-1)x+1=x−(−1), so a=−1a = -1a=−1 and the remainder is p(−1)=1−3−2−1=−5p(-1) = 1 - 3 - 2 - 1 = -5p(−1)=1−3−2−1=−5. With Ruffini on the coefficients 1,0,−3,2,−11, 0, -3, 2, -11,0,−3,2,−1 and a=−1a = -1a=−1 you get at the bottom 1,−1,−2,41, -1, -2, 41,−1,−2,4 and remainder −5-5−5.
  4. What is the multiplicity of the root 111 in the polynomial x4−x3−3x2+5x−2x^4 - x^3 - 3x^2 + 5x - 2x4−x3−3x2+5x−2?
    Dividing several times by x−1x - 1x−1 with Ruffini you get the quotients x3−3x+2x^3 - 3x + 2x3−3x+2, then x2+x−2x^2 + x - 2x2+x−2, then x+2x + 2x+2, which at 111 equals 3≠03 \neq 03=0. Three divisions: x4−x3−3x2+5x−2=(x−1)3(x+2)x^4 - x^3 - 3x^2 + 5x - 2 = (x - 1)^3(x + 2)x4−x3−3x2+5x−2=(x−1)3(x+2). Recognising a multiple root was also needed in problem 11 of the exam of 15/01/2026, where a determinant with a parameter had a double root.
  5. The quotient and remainder of the division of x3+2x2−x+3x^3 + 2x^2 - x + 3x3+2x2−x+3 by x2+1x^2 + 1x2+1 are:
    x3:x2=xx^3 : x^2 = xx3:x2=x, and (x3+2x2−x+3)−x(x2+1)=2x2−2x+3(x^3 + 2x^2 - x + 3) - x(x^2 + 1) = 2x^2 - 2x + 3(x3+2x2−x+3)−x(x2+1)=2x2−2x+3; then 2x2:x2=22x^2 : x^2 = 22x2:x2=2, and (2x2−2x+3)−2(x2+1)=−2x+1(2x^2 - 2x + 3) - 2(x^2 + 1) = -2x + 1(2x2−2x+3)−2(x2+1)=−2x+1, of degree 1<21 < 21<2. Watch out for the fourth answer: x⋅(x2+1)+(2x2−2x+3)x \cdot (x^2 + 1) + (2x^2 - 2x + 3)x⋅(x2+1)+(2x2−2x+3) really gives back the dividend, but the "remainder" has degree 222, not smaller than the divisor, so the division is not finished.
  6. A polynomial with real coefficients of degree 444 has the roots 1+i1 + i1+i and 2i2i2i. What are the other two roots?
    By Proposition 4.11 the conjugates 1+i‾=1−i\overline{1 + i} = 1 - i1+i​=1−i and 2i‾=−2i\overline{2i} = -2i2i=−2i are roots too. They are four distinct roots, and by the fundamental theorem a polynomial of degree 444 has no others. The monic polynomial is (x2−2x+2)(x2+4)=x4−2x3+6x2−8x+8(x^2 - 2x + 2)(x^2 + 4) = x^4 - 2x^3 + 6x^2 - 8x + 8(x2−2x+2)(x2+4)=x4−2x3+6x2−8x+8.
  7. In which of these polynomials is the number 222 a root with multiplicity exactly 222?
    (x2−4)(x+2)=(x−2)(x+2)2(x^2 - 4)(x + 2) = (x - 2)(x + 2)^2(x2−4)(x+2)=(x−2)(x+2)2: there 222 is simple (it is −2-2−2 that is double). In (x−2)3(x - 2)^3(x−2)3 the multiplicity is 333, in x2(x−2)x^2(x - 2)x2(x−2) it is 111; x2+4x^2 + 4x2+4 at 222 equals 888, so 222 is not even a root.
  8. Which of these polynomials belongs to R2[x]\R_2[x]R2​[x]?
    (x+1)2−x2=2x+1(x + 1)^2 - x^2 = 2x + 1(x+1)2−x2=2x+1 has degree 1≤21 \le 21≤2 and real coefficients. x3−1x^3 - 1x3−1 and (x−1)(x2+1)(x - 1)(x^2 + 1)(x−1)(x2+1) have degree 333; ix+1ix + 1ix+1 has a non-real coefficient (it belongs to C1[x]\C_1[x]C1​[x]); 1x+x\frac 1x + xx1​+x is not a polynomial. The space R2[x]\R_2[x]R2​[x] appears in many questions on subspaces, for example in the exams of 08/02/2024 and 05/02/2026 (question 2).
  9. The complex roots of z2−2z+5z^2 - 2z + 5z2−2z+5 are:
    Δ=4−20=−16\Delta = 4 - 20 = -16Δ=4−20=−16, with square roots ±4i\pm 4i±4i; so z±=2±4i2=1±2iz_\pm = \frac{2 \pm 4i}2 = 1 \pm 2iz±​=22±4i​=1±2i. Δ<0\Delta < 0Δ<0 only means that there are no real roots; the complex roots are conjugate because the coefficients are real. Similar to the exam of 02/09/2025 (question 4), where two eigenvalues were the complex conjugate roots of t2+2t+4t^2 + 2t + 4t2+2t+4.
  10. The polynomial x2−(1+i)x+ix^2 - (1 + i)x + ix2−(1+i)x+i has the root iii. Which statement is true?
    Dividing by x−ix - ix−i (or noting that the sum and product of the roots are 1+i1 + i1+i and iii) you find x2−(1+i)x+i=(x−i)(x−1)x^2 - (1 + i)x + i = (x - i)(x - 1)x2−(1+i)x+i=(x−i)(x−1). Proposition 4.11 does not apply, because the coefficients are not all real: indeed at −i-i−i the polynomial equals −2+2i≠0-2 + 2i \neq 0−2+2i=0. The degree is 222, so the roots counted with multiplicity are exactly two. In problem 11 of the exam of 03/06/2026 too, a polynomial with complex coefficients had iii and −i-i−i as roots with different multiplicities.

Exercises

with solutions

Note · The exercises of this lesson

The handouts have no exercise section for lesson 4: the exercises below were written for these notes, the last two modelled on the exam papers.

1 · Normal form, degree and sets of polynomials basic

Reduce to normal form and find the degree: (a) (x+1)2−(x−1)2(x + 1)^2 - (x - 1)^2(x+1)2−(x−1)2; (b) (x2+1)(x−1)−x3(x^2 + 1)(x - 1) - x^3(x2+1)(x−1)−x3; (c) 3x2y−2x2y+xy−x2y3x^2y - 2x^2y + xy - x^2y3x2y−2x2y+xy−x2y. Then say whether polynomials (a) and (b) belong to R1[x]\R_1[x]R1​[x], to R2[x]\R_2[x]R2​[x], to C2[x]\C_2[x]C2​[x].

Solution

(a) (x2+2x+1)−(x2−2x+1)=4x(x^2 + 2x + 1) - (x^2 - 2x + 1) = 4x(x2+2x+1)−(x2−2x+1)=4x: degree 111.

(b) (x2+1)(x−1)=x3−x2+x−1(x^2 + 1)(x - 1) = x^3 - x^2 + x - 1(x2+1)(x−1)=x3−x2+x−1, so the polynomial is −x2+x−1-x^2 + x - 1−x2+x−1: degree 222.

(c) The three monomials with literal part x2yx^2yx2y have coefficients 3−2−1=03 - 2 - 1 = 03−2−1=0 and disappear: what is left is xyxyxy, of degree 1+1=21 + 1 = 21+1=2.

Membership: (a) has degree 111, so it belongs to R1[x]\R_1[x]R1​[x], to R2[x]\R_2[x]R2​[x] and to C2[x]\C_2[x]C2​[x]. (b) has degree 222: it belongs to R2[x]\R_2[x]R2​[x] and to C2[x]\C_2[x]C2​[x], but not to R1[x]\R_1[x]R1​[x]. (Every Rk[x]\R_k[x]Rk​[x] is contained in Ck[x]\C_k[x]Ck​[x] and in Rk+1[x]\R_{k+1}[x]Rk+1​[x].)

2 · A long division basic

Divide x4−1x^4 - 1x4−1 by x2+x+1x^2 + x + 1x2+x+1 and check the result.

Solution

Dividend with the zeros: x4+0x3+0x2+0x−1x^4 + 0x^3 + 0x^2 + 0x - 1x4+0x3+0x2+0x−1.

  1. x4:x2=x2x^4 : x^2 = x^2x4:x2=x2. x2(x2+x+1)=x4+x3+x2x^2(x^2 + x + 1) = x^4 + x^3 + x^2x2(x2+x+1)=x4+x3+x2; subtracting, what is left is −x3−x2+0x−1-x^3 - x^2 + 0x - 1−x3−x2+0x−1.
  2. −x3:x2=−x-x^3 : x^2 = -x−x3:x2=−x. −x(x2+x+1)=−x3−x2−x-x(x^2 + x + 1) = -x^3 - x^2 - x−x(x2+x+1)=−x3−x2−x; subtracting, what is left is x−1x - 1x−1.
  3. x−1x - 1x−1 has degree 1<21 < 21<2: stop.

Quotient q(x)=x2−xq(x) = x^2 - xq(x)=x2−x, remainder r(x)=x−1r(x) = x - 1r(x)=x−1. Check: (x2−x)(x2+x+1)=x4+x3+x2−x3−x2−x=x4−x(x^2 - x)(x^2 + x + 1) = x^4 + x^3 + x^2 - x^3 - x^2 - x = x^4 - x(x2−x)(x2+x+1)=x4+x3+x2−x3−x2−x=x4−x, and x4−x+(x−1)=x4−1x^4 - x + (x - 1) = x^4 - 1x4−x+(x−1)=x4−1.

3 · Ruffini and complete factorisation basic

Check that 222 is a root of p(x)=x4−5x2+4p(x) = x^4 - 5x^2 + 4p(x)=x4−5x2+4, divide by x−2x - 2x−2 with Ruffini and factor p(x)p(x)p(x) into factors of degree one.

Solution

p(2)=16−20+4=0p(2) = 16 - 20 + 4 = 0p(2)=16−20+4=0. Ruffini on the coefficients 1,0,−5,0,41, 0, -5, 0, 41,0,−5,0,4 (watch out for the two zeros) with a=2a = 2a=2:

111000−5-5−5000444
a=2a = 2a=2222444−2-2−2−4-4−4
111222−1-1−1−2-2−2000

Quotient x3+2x2−x−2x^3 + 2x^2 - x - 2x3+2x2−x−2, remainder 000. Factoring by grouping: x2(x+2)−(x+2)=(x+2)(x2−1)=(x+2)(x−1)(x+1)x^2(x + 2) - (x + 2) = (x + 2)(x^2 - 1) = (x + 2)(x - 1)(x + 1)x2(x+2)−(x+2)=(x+2)(x2−1)=(x+2)(x−1)(x+1). So

x4−5x2+4=(x−2)(x+2)(x−1)(x+1).x^4 - 5x^2 + 4 = (x - 2)(x + 2)(x - 1)(x + 1).x4−5x2+4=(x−2)(x+2)(x−1)(x+1).

You could also start from t=x2t = x^2t=x2: t2−5t+4=(t−1)(t−4)t^2 - 5t + 4 = (t - 1)(t - 4)t2−5t+4=(t−1)(t−4), and then x2−1x^2 - 1x2−1 and x2−4x^2 - 4x2−4 factor as differences of squares.

4 · Roots and multiplicity intermediate

Find all the roots of p(x)=x3−3x+2p(x) = x^3 - 3x + 2p(x)=x3−3x+2 with their multiplicity.

Solution

Integer candidates: the divisors of 222, that is ±1,±2\pm 1, \pm 2±1,±2. p(1)=1−3+2=0p(1) = 1 - 3 + 2 = 0p(1)=1−3+2=0: a root. Ruffini on 1,0,−3,21, 0, -3, 21,0,−3,2 with a=1a = 1a=1: at the bottom 1,1,−21, 1, -21,1,−2 and remainder 000, quotient x2+x−2x^2 + x - 2x2+x−2. This equals 000 at 111 (1+1−2=01 + 1 - 2 = 01+1−2=0): Ruffini again, at the bottom 1,21, 21,2 and remainder 000, quotient x+2x + 2x+2, which at 111 equals 3≠03 \neq 03=0.

So p(x)=(x−1)2(x+2)p(x) = (x - 1)^2(x + 2)p(x)=(x−1)2(x+2): the root 111 has multiplicity 222 and the root −2-2−2 has multiplicity 111. Counted with multiplicity there are 2+1=32 + 1 = 32+1=3 roots, as many as the degree. It is the polynomial of the graph in the section on multiplicity.

5 · Imposing a double root intermediate

Find the real numbers aaa and bbb for which (x−1)2(x - 1)^2(x−1)2 divides x3+ax+bx^3 + ax + bx3+ax+b.

Solution

(x−1)2(x - 1)^2(x−1)2 divides the polynomial if and only if 111 is a root with multiplicity at least 222: the polynomial is divisible by x−1x - 1x−1 and the quotient still has the root 111.

  1. Ruffini on 1,0,a,b1, 0, a, b1,0,a,b with 111: at the bottom 111, 111, 1+a1 + a1+a and remainder 1+a+b1 + a + b1+a+b. The remainder must be 000: a+b=−1a + b = -1a+b=−1.
  2. The quotient is x2+x+(1+a)x^2 + x + (1 + a)x2+x+(1+a), and it must equal 000 at 111: 1+1+1+a=01 + 1 + 1 + a = 01+1+1+a=0, that is a=−3a = -3a=−3.
  3. Then b=−1−a=2b = -1 - a = 2b=−1−a=2.

The polynomial is x3−3x+2=(x−1)2(x+2)x^3 - 3x + 2 = (x - 1)^2(x + 2)x3−3x+2=(x−1)2(x+2), the one of the previous exercise.

6 · A second-degree equation with complex coefficients intermediate

Find the roots of z2+(2−i)z−2iz^2 + (2 - i)z - 2iz2+(2−i)z−2i.

Solution

a=1a = 1a=1, b=2−ib = 2 - ib=2−i, c=−2ic = -2ic=−2i.

  1. Δ=(2−i)2−4(−2i)=(4−4i+i2)+8i=3−4i+8i=3+4i\Delta = (2 - i)^2 - 4(-2i) = (4 - 4i + i^2) + 8i = 3 - 4i + 8i = 3 + 4iΔ=(2−i)2−4(−2i)=(4−4i+i2)+8i=3−4i+8i=3+4i.
  2. Square roots of 3+4i3 + 4i3+4i: I look for w=u+viw = u + viw=u+vi with w2=u2−v2+2uvi=3+4iw^2 = u^2 - v^2 + 2uvi = 3 + 4iw2=u2−v2+2uvi=3+4i, that is u2−v2=3u^2 - v^2 = 3u2−v2=3 and uv=2uv = 2uv=2. With u=2u = 2u=2, v=1v = 1v=1 it works: (2+i)2=4+4i−1=3+4i(2 + i)^2 = 4 + 4i - 1 = 3 + 4i(2+i)2=4+4i−1=3+4i. So ±w=±(2+i)\pm w = \pm(2 + i)±w=±(2+i).
  3. z±=−(2−i)±(2+i)2z_\pm = \frac{-(2 - i) \pm (2 + i)}2z±​=2−(2−i)±(2+i)​: with the plus, −2+i+2+i2=i\frac{-2 + i + 2 + i}2 = i2−2+i+2+i​=i; with the minus, −2+i−2−i2=−2\frac{-2 + i - 2 - i}2 = -22−2+i−2−i​=−2.

The roots are iii and −2-2−2: indeed (z−i)(z+2)=z2+2z−iz−2i=z2+(2−i)z−2i(z - i)(z + 2) = z^2 + 2z - iz - 2i = z^2 + (2 - i)z - 2i(z−i)(z+2)=z2+2z−iz−2i=z2+(2−i)z−2i. Here too −i-i−i is not a root: the coefficients are not real.

7 · A biquadratic, factored in R and in C intermediate

Find the roots of z4+3z2−4z^4 + 3z^2 - 4z4+3z2−4 and factor the polynomial into factors with real coefficients and then into factors of degree one with complex coefficients.

Solution

With t=z2t = z^2t=z2: t2+3t−4=(t+4)(t−1)t^2 + 3t - 4 = (t + 4)(t - 1)t2+3t−4=(t+4)(t−1), roots t=−4t = -4t=−4 and t=1t = 1t=1. So z2=1z^2 = 1z2=1 (that is z=±1z = \pm 1z=±1) or z2=−4z^2 = -4z2=−4 (that is z=±2iz = \pm 2iz=±2i).

  • In R\RR: z4+3z2−4=(z2−1)(z2+4)=(z−1)(z+1)(z2+4)z^4 + 3z^2 - 4 = (z^2 - 1)(z^2 + 4) = (z - 1)(z + 1)(z^2 + 4)z4+3z2−4=(z2−1)(z2+4)=(z−1)(z+1)(z2+4), where z2+4z^2 + 4z2+4 has Δ=−16<0\Delta = -16 < 0Δ=−16<0 and does not factor further in R\RR.
  • In C\CC: (z−1)(z+1)(z−2i)(z+2i)(z - 1)(z + 1)(z - 2i)(z + 2i)(z−1)(z+1)(z−2i)(z+2i).

Four roots, as many as the degree; the two non-real ones are conjugate, as Proposition 4.11 requires.

8 · All the roots, knowing one of them hard

Knowing that iii is a root of p(x)=x4−2x3+6x2−2x+5p(x) = x^4 - 2x^3 + 6x^2 - 2x + 5p(x)=x4−2x3+6x2−2x+5, find all the roots.

Solution
  1. The coefficients are real, so by Proposition 4.11 −i-i−i is a root too. Then (x−i)(x+i)=x2+1(x - i)(x + i) = x^2 + 1(x−i)(x+i)=x2+1 divides p(x)p(x)p(x).
  2. I divide by x2+1x^2 + 1x2+1: x4:x2=x2x^4 : x^2 = x^2x4:x2=x2, and p(x)−x2(x2+1)=−2x3+5x2−2x+5p(x) - x^2(x^2 + 1) = -2x^3 + 5x^2 - 2x + 5p(x)−x2(x2+1)=−2x3+5x2−2x+5; then −2x3:x2=−2x-2x^3 : x^2 = -2x−2x3:x2=−2x, and what is left is 5x2+55x^2 + 55x2+5; then 5x2:x2=55x^2 : x^2 = 55x2:x2=5, and what is left is 000. Quotient x2−2x+5x^2 - 2x + 5x2−2x+5.
  3. x2−2x+5x^2 - 2x + 5x2−2x+5: Δ=4−20=−16\Delta = 4 - 20 = -16Δ=4−20=−16, roots 2±4i2=1±2i\frac{2 \pm 4i}2 = 1 \pm 2i22±4i​=1±2i.

The roots are iii, −i-i−i, 1+2i1 + 2i1+2i, 1−2i1 - 2i1−2i, and p(x)=(x2+1)(x2−2x+5)p(x) = (x^2 + 1)(x^2 - 2x + 5)p(x)=(x2+1)(x2−2x+5).

9 · Building a polynomial from its roots hard

Find the monic polynomial with real coefficients of degree 333 that has the roots 222 and 1+i1 + i1+i. Is it unique?

Solution

Real coefficients, so 1−i1 - i1−i is a root too. A polynomial of degree 333 has exactly three roots counted with multiplicity (fundamental theorem), so they are 222, 1+i1 + i1+i, 1−i1 - i1−i, and the monic polynomial is

(x−2)(x−1−i)(x−1+i)=(x−2)(x2−2x+2)=x3−4x2+6x−4.(x - 2)(x - 1 - i)(x - 1 + i) = (x - 2)(x^2 - 2x + 2) = x^3 - 4x^2 + 6x - 4.(x−2)(x−1−i)(x−1+i)=(x−2)(x2−2x+2)=x3−4x2+6x−4.

Here (x−1−i)(x−1+i)=(x−1)2−i2=(x−1)2+1=x2−2x+2(x - 1 - i)(x - 1 + i) = (x - 1)^2 - i^2 = (x - 1)^2 + 1 = x^2 - 2x + 2(x−1−i)(x−1+i)=(x−1)2−i2=(x−1)2+1=x2−2x+2, as for every conjugate pair. It is unique: the three roots are forced, and a monic polynomial is determined by its roots (it is the product of the factors x−zkx - z_kx−zk​).

10 · A remainder without doing the division hard

Find the remainder of the division of p(x)=x100+1p(x) = x^{100} + 1p(x)=x100+1 by x2−1x^2 - 1x2−1.

Solution

The divisor has degree 222, so the remainder has degree at most 111: r(x)=ax+br(x) = ax + br(x)=ax+b, and

x100+1=q(x)(x2−1)+ax+b.x^{100} + 1 = q(x)(x^2 - 1) + ax + b.x100+1=q(x)(x2−1)+ax+b.

I substitute the roots of the divisor, where x2−1x^2 - 1x2−1 vanishes:

  • x=1x = 1x=1: 1+1=0+a+b1 + 1 = 0 + a + b1+1=0+a+b, that is a+b=2a + b = 2a+b=2;
  • x=−1x = -1x=−1: (−1)100+1=2=−a+b(-1)^{100} + 1 = 2 = -a + b(−1)100+1=2=−a+b.

Adding, 2b=42b = 42b=4, so b=2b = 2b=2 and a=0a = 0a=0. The remainder is the constant r(x)=2r(x) = 2r(x)=2. It is the same idea as in the proof of Proposition 4.2: you substitute a value that makes the divisor vanish.

11 · As at the exam: a determinant with a parameter exam style

In an exam problem the determinant of a matrix that depends on a real parameter kkk equals −k3+3k+2-k^3 + 3k + 2−k3+3k+2. For which values of kkk is the determinant non-zero? Which value of kkk is a double root?

Solution
  1. I look for a root among the divisors of the constant term 222: ±1,±2\pm 1, \pm 2±1,±2. With k=2k = 2k=2: −8+6+2=0-8 + 6 + 2 = 0−8+6+2=0. So (k−2)(k - 2)(k−2) divides the polynomial.
  2. Ruffini on the coefficients −1,0,3,2-1, 0, 3, 2−1,0,3,2 with a=2a = 2a=2: bring down −1-1−1; −1⋅2=−2-1 \cdot 2 = -2−1⋅2=−2 and 0−2=−20 - 2 = -20−2=−2; −2⋅2=−4-2 \cdot 2 = -4−2⋅2=−4 and 3−4=−13 - 4 = -13−4=−1; −1⋅2=−2-1 \cdot 2 = -2−1⋅2=−2 and 2−2=02 - 2 = 02−2=0. Quotient −k2−2k−1=−(k+1)2-k^2 - 2k - 1 = -(k + 1)^2−k2−2k−1=−(k+1)2.
  3. Factorisation: −k3+3k+2=−(k−2)(k+1)2-k^3 + 3k + 2 = -(k - 2)(k + 1)^2−k3+3k+2=−(k−2)(k+1)2.
  4. Conclusion: the determinant vanishes only for k=2k = 2k=2 and k=−1k = -1k=−1, and it is non-zero for every k≠2,−1k \neq 2, -1k=2,−1. The root −1-1−1 is double.

It is the scheme of problem 11 of the exam of 15/01/2026, where the determinant was another polynomial of degree three in kkk with a double root: you find a root by eye, divide, and factor the second-degree part.

12 · As at the exam: which one is a root exam style

Which of the following is a root of p(z)=z4−2z2−8p(z) = z^4 - 2z^2 - 8p(z)=z4−2z2−8? (a) z=i2z = i\sqrt 2z=i2​; (b) z=2iz = 2iz=2i; (c) z=2z = \sqrt 2z=2​; (d) z=1+iz = 1 + iz=1+i; (e) the polynomial has no roots.

Solution

By factoring. With t=z2t = z^2t=z2: t2−2t−8=(t−4)(t+2)t^2 - 2t - 8 = (t - 4)(t + 2)t2−2t−8=(t−4)(t+2), so z2=4z^2 = 4z2=4 or z2=−2z^2 = -2z2=−2: the roots are ±2\pm 2±2 and ±i2\pm i\sqrt 2±i2​. Answer (a).

By substituting the answers. (a) (i2)2=−2(i\sqrt 2)^2 = -2(i2​)2=−2 and (i2)4=4(i\sqrt 2)^4 = 4(i2​)4=4: p=4+4−8=0p = 4 + 4 - 8 = 0p=4+4−8=0. (b) (2i)2=−4(2i)^2 = -4(2i)2=−4 and (2i)4=16(2i)^4 = 16(2i)4=16: p=16+8−8=16p = 16 + 8 - 8 = 16p=16+8−8=16. (c) p(2)=4−4−8=−8p(\sqrt 2) = 4 - 4 - 8 = -8p(2​)=4−4−8=−8. (d) (1+i)2=2i(1 + i)^2 = 2i(1+i)2=2i and (1+i)4=−4(1 + i)^4 = -4(1+i)4=−4: p=−4−4i−8=−12−4ip = -4 - 4i - 8 = -12 - 4ip=−4−4i−8=−12−4i. (e) is false by the fundamental theorem. Here too the answer is (a).

§14

Review questions

self-check

Answer out loud or in writing, then open the answer.

What is the degree of a polynomial? Why must you first reduce it to normal form?

It is the largest degree of its monomials, once it is written in normal form (monomials with different literal parts and non-zero coefficients). You must reduce first because some terms can cancel out: (x+1)2−x2=2x+1(x + 1)^2 - x^2 = 2x + 1(x+1)2−x2=2x+1 has degree 111.

What are R[x]\R[x]R[x], C[x]\C[x]C[x] and Rk[x]\R_k[x]Rk​[x]?

The polynomials in one variable xxx with real coefficients, with complex coefficients, and with real coefficients of degree ≤k\le k≤k. R2[x]\R_2[x]R2​[x] also contains the constants and the zero polynomial.

What does division with remainder between polynomials say?

Given p(x)p(x)p(x) and d(x)≠0d(x) \neq 0d(x)=0, there exist unique q(x)q(x)q(x) and r(x)r(x)r(x) with p(x)=q(x)d(x)+r(x)p(x) = q(x)d(x) + r(x)p(x)=q(x)d(x)+r(x) and the degree of rrr strictly smaller than the degree of ddd.

When does a polynomial d(x)d(x)d(x) divide p(x)p(x)p(x)? Give an example.

When the division of p(x)p(x)p(x) by d(x)d(x)d(x) has zero remainder, that is p(x)=q(x)d(x)p(x) = q(x)d(x)p(x)=q(x)d(x). For example (x+1)∣(x3+1)(x + 1) \mid (x^3 + 1)(x+1)∣(x3+1), because x3+1=(x2−x+1)(x+1)x^3 + 1 = (x^2 - x + 1)(x + 1)x3+1=(x2−x+1)(x+1).

What is a root of a polynomial?

A number aaa such that p(a)=0p(a) = 0p(a)=0, that is a solution of the equation p(x)=0p(x) = 0p(x)=0 (Definition 4.1). It can be real or complex.

What does Proposition 4.2 say and how is it proved?

aaa is a root of p(x)p(x)p(x) if and only if (x−a)∣p(x)(x - a) \mid p(x)(x−a)∣p(x). You divide: p(x)=q(x)(x−a)+r0p(x) = q(x)(x - a) + r_0p(x)=q(x)(x−a)+r0​ with r0r_0r0​ constant (the remainder has degree smaller than 111); substituting x=ax = ax=a you get p(a)=r0p(a) = r_0p(a)=r0​. So p(a)=0p(a) = 0p(a)=0 if and only if the remainder is zero.

What is the remainder of the division of p(x)p(x)p(x) by x−ax - ax−a?

It is p(a)p(a)p(a): it is the central step of the proof of Proposition 4.2. For example the remainder of 2x3−3x2+4x−52x^3 - 3x^2 + 4x - 52x3−3x2+4x−5 divided by x−2x - 2x−2 is p(2)=7p(2) = 7p(2)=7.

What is the multiplicity of a root and how is it computed?

It is the largest kkk for which (x−a)k(x - a)^k(x−a)k divides p(x)p(x)p(x) (Definition 4.3). It is computed by dividing by x−ax - ax−a several times, until aaa is no longer a root of the quotient.

How many roots can a polynomial of degree n≥1n \ge 1n≥1 have? And in the complex numbers?

At most nnn, counted with multiplicity (Theorem 4.6). In the complex numbers exactly nnn, counted with multiplicity (Theorem 4.8, fundamental theorem of algebra).

How do you solve ax2+bx+c=0ax^2 + bx + c = 0ax2+bx+c=0 in the complex numbers?

With the formula x±=−b±Δ2ax_\pm = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt\Delta}{2a}x±​=2a−b±Δ​​, Δ=b2−4ac\Delta = b^2 - 4acΔ=b2−4ac, where ±Δ\pm\sqrt\Delta±Δ​ are the two complex square roots of Δ\DeltaΔ (Example 4.9). For example the roots of x2+2x+5x^2 + 2x + 5x2+2x+5 are −1±2i-1 \pm 2i−1±2i.

What does Proposition 4.11 say? Why are real coefficients needed?

If p(x)p(x)p(x) has real coefficients and p(z)=0p(z) = 0p(z)=0, then also p(zˉ)=0p(\bar z) = 0p(zˉ)=0. In the proof you conjugate p(z)=0p(z) = 0p(z)=0 and use aˉi=ai\bar a_i = a_iaˉi​=ai​, which holds only for real coefficients: x2+(1−i)x−ix^2 + (1 - i)x - ix2+(1−i)x−i has the root iii but not −i-i−i.

Why does a real polynomial of odd degree have at least one real root?

Because it has nnn complex roots (an odd number) and the non-real ones come in conjugate pairs (an even number): at least one must be real.

§15

Glossary

terms
Monomial
Product of a numerical coefficient and a literal part, like −2xy-2xy−2xy; the degree is the sum of the exponents.
Polynomial
Sum of monomials, like 7+3x2−2 y37 + 3x^2 - \sqrt 2\,y^37+3x2−2​y3.
Normal form
Way of writing a polynomial as a sum of monomials with different literal parts and non-zero coefficients (or the polynomial 000).
Degree
The largest degree of the monomials of a polynomial in normal form.
Constant term
The coefficient a0a_0a0​, the monomial of degree zero.
Monic polynomial
Polynomial whose highest-degree term has coefficient 111.
R[x]\R[x]R[x], C[x]\C[x]C[x]
Polynomials in one variable with real, complex coefficients.
Rk[x]\R_k[x]Rk​[x]
Real polynomials of degree at most kkk (including the zero polynomial).
Division with remainder
p(x)=q(x)d(x)+r(x)p(x) = q(x)d(x) + r(x)p(x)=q(x)d(x)+r(x) with deg⁡r<deg⁡d\deg r < \deg ddegr<degd: qqq quotient, rrr remainder.
Divisibility
d(x)∣p(x)d(x) \mid p(x)d(x)∣p(x): the division has zero remainder, that is p(x)=q(x)d(x)p(x) = q(x)d(x)p(x)=q(x)d(x).
Ruffini's rule
Scheme with only the coefficients for dividing by x−ax - ax−a; the last number is the remainder, equal to p(a)p(a)p(a).
Root
A number aaa with p(a)=0p(a) = 0p(a)=0 (Definition 4.1).
Multiplicity
The largest kkk for which (x−a)k(x - a)^k(x−a)k divides p(x)p(x)p(x) (Definition 4.3); simple, double, triple root.
Discriminant
Δ=b2−4ac\Delta = b^2 - 4acΔ=b2−4ac for ax2+bx+cax^2 + bx + cax2+bx+c; among the reals it decides how many roots there are.
Fundamental theorem of algebra
Every polynomial with complex coefficients of degree nnn has exactly nnn complex roots, counted with multiplicity (Theorem 4.8).
Conjugate roots
If the coefficients are real and zzz is a root, so is zˉ\bar zzˉ (Proposition 4.11).
Biquadratic equation
Equation with only even powers, like z4+5z2+4=0z^4 + 5z^2 + 4 = 0z4+5z2+4=0: it is solved with t=z2t = z^2t=z2.
